question.prompt:
Elijah has a large collection of identical wooden cubes which are plain on \(4\) faces and shaded on \(2\) faces that share an edge. He glues some cubes together face-to-face. The figure below shows \(2\) cubes being glued together, leaving \(3\) shaded faces visible. What is the fewest number of cubes that he could glue together to ensure that no shaded faces are visible, no matter how he rotates the figure?

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
To prove a minimum, we need both a working arrangement and a reason fewer cubes cannot work.

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

One cube leaves both shaded faces exposed. Two cubes have just one face-to-face contact, which covers only one face of each cube. Each cube therefore still has at least one shaded face exposed.

Now consider three cubes joined into one piece. Some cube must have the other two attached to it. Those two cubes occupy either opposite faces or adjacent faces of the middle cube. In the opposite case, they are separated by the middle cube. In the adjacent case, they meet only along an edge. Thus they cannot share a full face with each other. Each has only one glued face, leaving at least one of its two shaded faces exposed and visible from some direction. Three cubes cannot work.

Four cubes do work. Arrange them in a single layer forming a \(2\times2\) block. Each cube touches two neighbors on two faces that share an edge. Orient each cube so that its two shaded faces are precisely those two contact faces. All shaded faces are then hidden at glued contacts, and every exterior face is plain. Rotating the block cannot reveal any shading.

Therefore the fewest number is \(4\) cubes, choice A.
solutions.title: Rule out smaller assemblies and construct four
